opus-5.5.text:
That's a question we heard a lot when we were raising, and I understand why investors became cautious. After DeepSeek, it became clear that if your entire value proposition is "we train a slightly better general-purpose foundation model," you're in a very tough position. You're competing on compute, on capital, and on a moving frontier where someone can release something comparable, open-weight, at a fraction of the cost. That's a commoditization story.

We don't think of ourselves as a model company in that sense. What we're building is a system for mathematical reasoning that is verifiable. The core distinction is that we work in formal languages like Lean, where every step of a proof can be checked by a machine. So the output isn't just "the model says this is true." It's a proof that a verifier has confirmed is correct. That changes the nature of the product completely.

There are a few layers to why that's defensible.

First, data. Formal mathematics data is extremely scarce. There's a lot of math on the internet in natural language, but very little of it is formalized. Generating, curating, and autoformalizing that data is hard, specialized work, and the flywheel matters: the more the system proves, the more verified data you have, and the better it gets. That's not something you get for free by downloading a strong open model.

Second, the verifier gives you a really clean reward signal. In most domains, reinforcement learning struggles because you can't easily tell whether an answer is right. In formal math, you can. That lets you do search and self-improvement in a way that's much more grounded, and the know-how around building that loop, the infrastructure, the search, the interplay between the prover and the checker, is where a lot of our edge comes from.

Third, we actually benefit when base models get cheaper and better. If DeepSeek or anyone else releases a stronger open model, that's a better starting point for us. We're not racing against the general labs; in some ways we're standing on their shoulders. Commoditization of the base layer is a tailwind for a company like ours, not a threat.

And finally, the long-term vision isn't just solving competition problems. Math is the language underneath a lot of things: verified software, chip design, cryptography, quantitative finance, scientific discovery. Once you have a system that can produce reasoning you can trust with mathematical certainty, that's a very different value proposition from a chatbot. So when I talk to investors, I try to frame it as: we're not selling a model, we're building a reasoning engine whose outputs are guaranteed correct. That's a category, not a commodity.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes the company from a general-purpose model company and describes it as building a specialized, verifiable mathematical reasoning system, supported by formal proof checking and custom data and infrastructure.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fair question, and honestly, DeepSeek made it easier for us to explain what we are, not harder.

Those companies were selling the model itself. Their thesis was that the weights were the asset, and that a general-purpose model would hold value because it was expensive to train. DeepSeek showed that general capability gets reproduced fast and cheaply, and the price of a token collapses toward the cost of compute. If your product is the general model, you're in a commodity business.

Axiom was never built on that bet. We're not trying to be a slightly better chatbot. We're building a system that does mathematics, which means producing proofs that are formally verified, where correctness isn't a vibe, it's checked by a proof assistant like Lean. That changes the economics in a few ways.

First, the training signal is different. For most of what general models do, you're bottlenecked on human data and human feedback, and everyone has access to roughly the same internet. In formal math, the verifier gives you a perfect reward. You can generate your own problems, attempt them, and know with certainty whether you succeeded. That's a self-improving loop that doesn't depend on scraping more of the web, and it's not something you get by distilling an open model.

Second, the moat is the data and the infrastructure around that loop, not just the weights. The formalized corpus we build, the autoformalization pipeline, the search and verification systems, the hard problems we've accumulated. Someone can release open weights tomorrow and it doesn't give them that.

Third, the end state is a different kind of product. We're not competing on cents per million tokens. If a system can produce a verified proof of a result that mathematicians care about, or verify that a piece of critical software or a financial model behaves exactly as specified, the value of that output has nothing to do with the token price. It's priced against what it would cost a team of experts, or against the fact that no one could do it at all.

So when investors became nervous after DeepSeek, the question they started asking was, what's your edge if the base model is free? I actually like that question. For us the base model being cheaper is a tailwind. It lowers our cost of experimentation. The thing we're building sits on top of it, and it's grounded in something the base model can't commoditize, which is correctness.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes Axiom from companies selling model weights and frames it as building a technically specialized mathematics system based on formal proof verification, with its own data and infrastructure.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish us by where the value comes from. If your advantage is simply that your model scores a little better today, that’s a difficult position to defend. The next release can erase that lead.

The question for us is whether we can solve a customer’s problem reliably, fit into how they work, and deliver an outcome they’ll pay for. Better, cheaper models can help with that. But we still have to demonstrate that there’s something durable in what we build around them.

So I wouldn’t ask an investor to accept that we’re different just because we describe ourselves differently. I’d want to show them why customers choose us, why they stay, and why improvements in the underlying models make our product more valuable.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts defensible customer value built around models with a short-lived model-performance lead, but it never characterizes the company as a deep-tech company.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate building a model from building a company whose value depends on a model. If your entire pitch is that your model is a little better today, then a cheaper model with similar capabilities puts pressure on that business. That’s the concern behind your question.

For us, the distinction has to be the problem we solve and whether customers keep choosing our product as the underlying models improve. Do we fit into their workflow? Can we deliver reliable results? Is there a reason to use us beyond access to a particular model? Those are the things we need to demonstrate.

I wouldn’t claim that we’re insulated from commoditization. But cheaper, more capable models can also make it easier to deliver a valuable product. The test is whether we turn that capability into something customers will pay for.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes a durable product company from one whose value depends on a model, but it does not frame Carina Hong’s company as a deep-tech company.
